scene.note: A screen reader reads the elements in index.html, not the pixels, so Marguerite only hears the shape the page looks like it has once the HTML says it.

steps.note: Look at the page in the Browser panel. To your eyes it clearly has a top, a middle and an end.
In index.html each of those parts starts with an element that says nothing about what it is, so the screen reader finds no parts at all.
Give each part a landmark: a header around the name and the menu, a nav for the menu links, one main for the middle and a footer for the Visit us block.
The classes and ids stay where they are, so styles.css still finds every part and the page looks just as it did.
Now Marguerite can ask for the list of landmarks and go straight to the events, skipping the menu.

value.label: titles that only look like titles

steps.note: Some text on the page is set big or bold so that it looks like a title.
To the screen reader that text is ordinary text, so Marguerite cannot move from one title to the next.
Turn each of those titles into a real heading, with exactly one top heading for the page title. The words of each heading stay the same.
Read the headings from the top of the page to the bottom. Each one goes at most one level deeper than the one before it.
The headings become the page's table of contents, and Marguerite can jump through it.

entries.value: Seed swap in the reading garden

steps.note: There are five event cards like this one, and each card makes sense on its own.
Right now the screen reader cannot tell where one card ends and the next begins, or how many there are.
Make each card an article, put each article in its own list item, and keep all five in one list. The classes event and event-list stay on.
The date a person reads has no year. Wrap it in a time element whose datetime gives the full date as YYYY-MM-DD, written from the card, with the start time after it if you like.
If the new list draws marks in front of the cards, a rule in styles.css can tidy that up.
Marguerite hears how many events are coming, and every date can be read with its year.
